subject: math
domain: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability
cluster: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
intro: A two-way frequency table sorts each member of a group by two categories at once, like class and sport. The row totals, column totals, and grand total turn the table into a sample space you can read probabilities from. A single row or column total over the grand total is a marginal probability $P(A)$; a single cell over the grand total is a joint probability $P(A \cap B)$; and a cell over its row or column total is a conditional probability $P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}$. Two events are independent when $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$, or equivalently when $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$ (knowing one category does not change the chance of the other).

items.prompt: Of $40$ students surveyed, $22$ are seniors and the rest are juniors. Among the seniors, $15$ play a sport; among the juniors, $9$ play a sport. Build the two-way table of class (senior/junior) versus sport (yes/no) and find every row total, column total, and the grand total.

steps: Seniors total $22$. If $15$ seniors play a sport, then $22 - 15 = 7$ seniors do not.
Juniors total $40 - 22 = 18$. If $9$ juniors play a sport, then $18 - 9 = 9$ juniors do not.
Sport 'yes' column total: $15 + 9 = 24$. Sport 'no' column total: $7 + 9 = 16$.
Check the grand total both ways: rows give $22 + 18 = 40$; columns give $24 + 16 = 40$. They agree.
Completed table: Seniors $15$ yes, $7$ no ($22$); Juniors $9$ yes, $9$ no ($18$); columns $24$ yes, $16$ no; grand total $40$.
solution.answer: Seniors: $15$ sport, $7$ no sport, row total $22$. Juniors: $9$ sport, $9$ no sport, row total $18$. Columns: $24$ sport, $16$ no sport. Grand total $40$.

items.prompt: Using the completed table from Example 1 (grand total $40$, with $24$ students playing a sport and $22$ seniors), find the marginal probability $P(\text{plays a sport})$ and the joint probability $P(\text{senior and plays a sport})$.

steps: A marginal probability is a row or column total over the grand total. The 'sport yes' column total is $24$.
$P(\text{plays a sport}) = \dfrac{24}{40} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.
A joint probability is a single cell over the grand total. The 'senior and sport' cell holds $15$.
$P(\text{senior and plays a sport}) = \dfrac{15}{40} = \dfrac{3}{8}$.
solution.answer: $P(\text{plays a sport}) = \dfrac{3}{5}$ and $P(\text{senior and plays a sport}) = \dfrac{3}{8}$.

items.prompt: Using the same table ($15$ of the $22$ seniors play a sport, and $24$ of the $40$ students play a sport), find $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior})$ and $P(\text{senior} \mid \text{plays a sport})$. Explain why the two answers differ.

steps: A conditional probability uses a reduced sample space: the cell count over the conditioning total.
For $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior})$, condition on seniors, so the denominator is the senior row total $22$. The cell is $15$: $P = \dfrac{15}{22}$.
For $P(\text{senior} \mid \text{plays a sport})$, condition on sport-players, so the denominator is the sport column total $24$. The same cell is $15$: $P = \dfrac{15}{24} = \dfrac{5}{8}$.
The cell ($15$) is the same, but the conditioning total changes ($22$ seniors versus $24$ sport-players), so the two conditionals are different. The condition determines the denominator.
solution.answer: $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior}) = \dfrac{15}{22}$ and $P(\text{senior} \mid \text{plays a sport}) = \dfrac{5}{8}$; they differ because each conditions on a different total.

items.prompt: For the same table, test whether the events 'is a senior' and 'plays a sport' are independent using the product rule $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$. State a conclusion in context.

steps: Compute the marginals: $P(\text{senior}) = \dfrac{22}{40} = 0.55$ and $P(\text{sport}) = \dfrac{24}{40} = 0.6$.
Multiply them: $P(\text{senior})\cdot P(\text{sport}) = \dfrac{22}{40}\cdot\dfrac{24}{40} = \dfrac{528}{1600} = \dfrac{33}{100} = 0.33$.
Find the actual joint probability from the cell: $P(\text{senior and sport}) = \dfrac{15}{40} = \dfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$.
Compare: $0.375 \ne 0.33$, so $P(A \cap B) \ne P(A)\cdot P(B)$.

Conclusion: the events are not independent. Seniors play a sport more often than the product rule predicts, so knowing a student is a senior raises the chance they play a sport. Class and sport are dependent.
solution.answer: $P(A)\cdot P(B) = \dfrac{33}{100} = 0.33$ but $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$; since they are unequal, the events are dependent.

items.prompt: A two-way table for $200$ people classifies them by coffee drinker (yes/no) and morning person (yes/no). It is partly given: $80$ are coffee drinkers, $120$ are morning people, and the 'coffee and morning person' cell holds $48$. Test independence by comparing $P(\text{morning} \mid \text{coffee})$ with $P(\text{morning})$.

steps: Conditional probability: condition on coffee drinkers, so the denominator is $80$. The 'coffee and morning' cell is $48$.
$P(\text{morning} \mid \text{coffee}) = \dfrac{48}{80} = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6$.
Marginal probability: $P(\text{morning}) = \dfrac{120}{200} = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6$.
Compare: $P(\text{morning} \mid \text{coffee}) = 0.6 = P(\text{morning})$. They are exactly equal.
Conclusion: knowing someone drinks coffee does not change the chance they are a morning person, so being a coffee drinker and being a morning person are independent.
solution.answer: $P(\text{morning} \mid \text{coffee}) = \dfrac{3}{5} = P(\text{morning})$, so the events are independent.

items.prompt: A group of $50$ pets is sorted by type (cat/dog) and whether it has been microchipped. There are $30$ dogs, of which $24$ are chipped; among the cats, $11$ are chipped. Complete the two-way table with all row totals, column totals, and the grand total.
items.hint: There are $50 - 30 = 20$ cats. Subtract the chipped count from each row total to get the 'not chipped' count, then add down each column.

steps: Cats total $50 - 30 = 20$. Chipped cats $= 11$, so not chipped $= 20 - 11 = 9$.
Dogs total $30$. Chipped dogs $= 24$, so not chipped $= 30 - 24 = 6$.
Chipped column total: $24 + 11 = 35$. Not chipped column total: $6 + 9 = 15$.
Check: rows $30 + 20 = 50$; columns $35 + 15 = 50$. They agree, grand total $50$.
solution.answer: Dogs: $24$ chipped, $6$ not, total $30$. Cats: $11$ chipped, $9$ not, total $20$. Columns: $35$ chipped, $15$ not. Grand total $50$.

items.prompt: Using the completed pet table (grand total $50$, with $35$ chipped pets and the 'dog and chipped' cell equal to $24$), find $P(\text{chipped})$ and $P(\text{dog and chipped})$.
items.hint: Marginal probability is a column total over the grand total; joint probability is a single cell over the grand total.

steps: $P(\text{chipped})$ uses the chipped column total $35$ over the grand total: $\dfrac{35}{50} = \dfrac{7}{10}$.
$P(\text{dog and chipped})$ uses the single cell $24$ over the grand total: $\dfrac{24}{50} = \dfrac{12}{25}$.

items.prompt: From the same pet table ($24$ of the $30$ dogs are chipped, and $35$ of the $50$ pets are chipped), find $P(\text{chipped} \mid \text{dog})$ and $P(\text{dog} \mid \text{chipped})$.
items.hint: Each conditional is the 'dog and chipped' cell over the conditioning total. For $P(\text{chipped} \mid \text{dog})$ divide by the dog row total; for $P(\text{dog} \mid \text{chipped})$ divide by the chipped column total.

steps: $P(\text{chipped} \mid \text{dog})$ conditions on dogs, so the denominator is the dog row total $30$. The cell is $24$: $\dfrac{24}{30} = \dfrac{4}{5}$.
$P(\text{dog} \mid \text{chipped})$ conditions on chipped pets, so the denominator is the chipped column total $35$. The same cell is $24$: $\dfrac{24}{35}$ (already in lowest terms).
The cell stays $24$, but the conditioning total changes, so the two conditionals differ.

items.prompt: A survey of $80$ commuters records mode (bus/train) and whether each was late. There are $50$ bus riders, of whom $20$ were late; among the train riders, $6$ were late. Test whether 'rides the bus' and 'was late' are independent using $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$, and state a conclusion in context.
items.hint: First complete the table to find the total number late, then compare $P(\text{bus and late})$ with $P(\text{bus})\cdot P(\text{late})$.

steps: Train riders total $80 - 50 = 30$. Total late $= 20 + 6 = 26$.
Marginals: $P(\text{bus}) = \dfrac{50}{80} = \dfrac{5}{8} = 0.625$ and $P(\text{late}) = \dfrac{26}{80} = \dfrac{13}{40} = 0.325$.
Product: $P(\text{bus})\cdot P(\text{late}) = \dfrac{5}{8}\cdot\dfrac{13}{40} = \dfrac{65}{320} = \dfrac{13}{64} \approx 0.203$.
Actual joint: the 'bus and late' cell is $20$, so $P(\text{bus and late}) = \dfrac{20}{80} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$.
Compare: $0.25 \ne 0.203$, so $P(A \cap B) \ne P(A)\cdot P(B)$.
Conclusion: the events are dependent. Bus riders were late more often than the product rule predicts, so knowing a commuter rode the bus raises the chance they were late.
solution.answer: $P(\text{bus})\cdot P(\text{late}) = \dfrac{13}{64} \approx 0.203$ but $P(\text{bus and late}) = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$; since they are unequal, riding the bus and being late are dependent.

items.prompt: A two-way table for $120$ shoppers classifies them by membership (member/non-member) and whether they used a coupon. There are $60$ members and $40$ coupon users total. Fill in the 'member and coupon' cell so that membership and coupon use are independent, then give that cell count.
items.hint: Independence means $P(\text{member and coupon}) = P(\text{member})\cdot P(\text{coupon})$. Multiply that probability by the grand total to recover the cell count.

steps: Marginals: $P(\text{member}) = \dfrac{60}{120} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(\text{coupon}) = \dfrac{40}{120} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.
For independence, $P(\text{member and coupon}) = P(\text{member})\cdot P(\text{coupon}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{6}$.
Convert the joint probability back to a count: cell $= \dfrac{1}{6}\times 120 = 20$.
Check: with $20$ member coupon users, $P(\text{coupon} \mid \text{member}) = \dfrac{20}{60} = \dfrac{1}{3} = P(\text{coupon})$, confirming independence.
solution.answer: The 'member and coupon' cell must be $20$.
